title: A quicksort that survives anything
description:
Write a quicksort that stays fast on sorted, reversed and all-equal inputs, and a quickselect:

```cpp
std::pair<int, int> partition3(std::vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi, int pivot);   // Dutch national flag on a[lo..hi]
void quickSort(std::vector<int>& a);
int kthSmallest(std::vector<int> a, int k);                                          // k counts from 0
```

- `partition3` rearranges `a[lo..hi]` (inclusive) into elements `< pivot`, then `== pivot`, then `> pivot`, and returns the first and last index of the middle part. If no element equals the pivot, the middle part is empty and the pair is `(first index of the > part, that index - 1)`.
- `quickSort` picks a **random** element of the range as the pivot (seed a `std::mt19937` with any fixed number), partitions three ways, and recurses only on the `<` and `>` parts. Recurse on the smaller part and loop on the larger one.
- `kthSmallest` uses the same partitioning but continues into one part only: expected O(n). `k` outside `[0, size)` throws `std::out_of_range`.

The tests sort 100,000 already sorted, reversed and identical values. A last-element pivot or two-way partitioning takes O(n²) on some of them and times out.
hints: `partition3` keeps three boundaries: `a[lo..lt)` is less, `a[lt..i)` equal, `a(gt..hi]` greater, and `a[i..gt]` not yet looked at. An element bigger than the pivot is swapped to `gt` and `i` stays put, because the element swapped in has not been looked at yet.
Pick the pivot **value** first (`a[randomIn(lo, hi)]`), then partition around that value; you do not need to know where the pivot ends up.
rules: Write the partitioning and sorting yourself.
